stemMd: Which statement correctly distinguishes a virus from a bacterium?

options.label: A
options.textMd: A virus reproduces by binary fission when given nutrients.

options.label: B
options.textMd: A virus has a cell wall containing peptidoglycan, which a bacterium lacks.

options.label: C
options.textMd: A virus can replicate only inside a host cell, because it has no ribosomes or metabolism of its own.

options.label: D
options.textMd: A virus carries both DNA and RNA as its genetic material, whereas a bacterium carries only DNA.

options.label: E
options.textMd: A virus is larger than a bacterium and can be seen with an ordinary light microscope.

explanationMd:
A virus is not a cell. It is a nucleic acid genome (DNA or RNA, one type only) packed in a protein coat, sometimes with an outer envelope. It has no ribosomes and no metabolism, so it can only be copied by the machinery of a host cell.

A bacterium is a complete prokaryotic cell: it has ribosomes, its own metabolism, a DNA genome and a cell wall containing peptidoglycan, and it multiplies by binary fission. Test each statement against this contrast: peptidoglycan and binary fission belong to bacteria, a virus has a single type of nucleic acid, and viruses are much smaller than bacteria.

distractorRationale.b: This reverses the facts. Peptidoglycan is a component of bacterial cell walls, and a virus has no cell wall at all.
distractorRationale.a: Binary fission is how bacteria divide, in nutrient medium on their own. A virus is not a cell and cannot divide.
distractorRationale.d: A virus particle contains one kind of nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, never both as its genome. Bacteria have a DNA genome.
distractorRationale.e: Viruses are typically far smaller than bacteria and generally too small to see with a light microscope.

accessibilityText: A short text question with no figure. The question asks which statement correctly distinguishes a virus from a bacterium. The five choices say that a virus: reproduces by binary fission when given nutrients; has a peptidoglycan cell wall that a bacterium lacks; can replicate only inside a host cell because it has no ribosomes or metabolism of its own; carries both DNA and RNA while a bacterium carries only DNA; is larger than a bacterium and visible with an ordinary light microscope.

provenance.notes: Original item. Four distractors are true statements about bacteria or false statements about viruses that students commonly confuse.

review.author: tolc-f-wave6-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites with no ribosomes or metabolism. Binary fission is bacterial. Peptidoglycan is in bacteria, not viruses (the option reverses this). Viruses carry DNA or RNA, not usually both. Viruses are smaller than bacteria and not visible with a light microscope. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave6-tolcf-bio-run19) reached the same answer: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites with no ribosomes or metabolism of their own. Binary fission (a) is bacterial. Option b reverses which one has peptidoglycan. Viruses carry either DNA or RNA, not both, so d is false. Viruses are generally smaller than bacteria, so e is false.]
